claim: Small RNA next-generation sequencing of resting and activated human NK cells and their secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) led to the identification of a specific repertoire of NK-EV-associated microRNAs and their post-transcriptional modifications signature.
source: Small RNA next-generation sequencing of resting and activated human NK cells and their secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) led to the identification of a specific repertoire of NK-EV-associated microRNAs and their post-transcriptional modifications signature.
evidence: The manuscript describes performing small RNA sequencing experiments on NK cells and EVs, with results presented in figures and supplementary files.

claim: Several microRNAs of NK-EVs, namely miR-10b-5p, miR-92a-3p, and miR-155-5p, specifically target molecules involved in Th1 responses.
source: Several microRNAs of NK-EVs, namely miR-10b-5p, miR-92a-3p, and miR-155-5p, specifically target molecules involved in Th1 responses.
evidence: The manuscript presents in silico target analysis and experimental validation showing these miRNAs target Th1-related molecules.

claim: NK-EVs promote the downregulation of GATA3 mRNA in CD4+ T cells and subsequent TBX21 de-repression that leads to Th1 polarization and IFN-γ and IL-2 production.
source: NK-EVs promote the downregulation of GATA3 mRNA in CD4+ T cells and subsequent TBX21 de-repression that leads to Th1 polarization and IFN-γ and IL-2 production.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing GATA3 downregulation and TBX21 upregulation, along with flow cytometry and ELISA data showing increased IFN-γ and IL-2.

claim: NK-EVs have an effect on monocyte and moDCs (monocyte-derived dendritic cells) function, driving their activation and increased presentation and costimulatory functions.
source: NK-EVs also have an effect on monocyte and moDCs (monocyte-derived dendritic cells) function, driving their activation and increased presentation and costimulatory functions.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased MHC-II and CD86 expression on monocytes and moDCs after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Nanoparticle-delivered NK-EV microRNAs partially recapitulate NK-EV effects in mice.
source: Nanoparticle-delivered NK-EV microRNAs partially recapitulate NK-EV effects in mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents in vivo mouse experiments showing that nanoparticles carrying NK-EV miRNAs induce similar effects to NK-EVs on T cell activation and IFN-γ production.

claim: A total of 130 miRNAs were differentially expressed between activated NK cells and NK-EV released miRNAs; 96 miRNAs being enriched in NK-EVs and 34 miRNAs being more abundant in NK cells than in NK-EVs.
source: A total of 130 miRNAs were differentially expressed between activated NK cells and NK-EV released miRNAs; 96 miRNAs being enriched in NK-EVs and 34 miRNAs being more abundant in NK cells than in NK-EVs (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing data with statistical analysis showing differential expression between NK cells and NK-EVs, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The repertoire found in resting NK cells was different from that of in vitro-activated NK cells.
source: Also, the repertoire found in resting NK cells was different from that of in vitro-activated NK cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing data comparing resting and activated NK cells, shown in heatmaps and supplementary files.

claim: A total of 70 miRNAs were upregulated upon activation, while 98 miRNAs decreased their levels after cytokine stimulation.
source: A total of 70 miRNAs were upregulated upon activation, while 98 miRNAs decreased their levels after cytokine stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing data with statistical analysis comparing resting and activated NK cells.

claim: NK cells enriched from PBMCs by adding IL-12 and IL-18 with irradiated feeder cells for 6 days resulted in greater than 95% purity in all experiments.
source: Dot plots show the enrichment of CD3- CD56+ NK cells after 6–8 days culture with cytokines and irradiated feeder cells (left panel) and NK cell isolation (right panel), being greater than 95% in all experiments.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing NK cell purity after isolation, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Vesicles isolated from activated NK cells showed a mode size ranging from 165 to 209 nm among donors.
source: Vesicles isolated from activated NK cells were characterized using NanoSight showing a mode size ranging from 165 to 209 nm among donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: The manuscript presents NanoSight analysis data showing the size distribution of isolated NK-EVs.

claim: NK-EVs express the exosomal markers CD63 and Tsg101 and lack the EV-excluded marker Calnexin.
source: Also, biochemical analyses showed the NK-EV expression of the exosomal markers CD63 and Tsg101 and the absence of the EV-excluded marker Calnexin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data showing the presence of exosomal markers and absence of Calnexin in NK-EV preparations.

claim: Electron microscopy of isolated NK-EVs confirmed the presence of nano-sized membranous vesicles with their typical cup-shaped morphology.
source: In line with this, electron microscopy of isolated NK-EVs confirmed the presence of nano-sized membranous vesicles with their typical cup-shaped morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy images showing the morphology of isolated NK-EVs.

claim: Activated NK cells release more EVs than resting NK cells.
source: Analyses of the small EVs released from either resting or activated NK cells showed increased EV release upon activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: The manuscript presents nanoparticle-tracking analysis and dot blot data comparing EV release from resting and activated NK cells.

claim: EVs released from resting NK cells were barely detected using nanoparticle-tracking analysis (NTA) and dot blot techniques.
source: Indeed, EVs released from resting NK cells were barely detected using nanoparticle-tracking analysis (NTA) and dot blot techniques, for this reason they were not included in the study.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations from NTA and dot blot analyses.

claim: Differential expression of miRNAs between activated NK cells and NK-EVs suggests the existence of mechanisms of specific miRNAs sorting into EVs derived from NK cells.
source: Such differential expression suggested the existence of mechanisms of specific miRNAs sorting into EVs derived from NK cells, in agreement with published data (Mateescu et al., 2017; Villarroya-Beltri et al., 2013; Szostak et al., 2014; Batagov et al., 2011; Mittelbrunn et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression data and cites previous literature supporting the concept of selective miRNA sorting.

claim: Extensive miRNA remodelling occurs upon T lymphocyte activation.
source: These data are in agreement with extensive miRNA remodelling occurring upon T lymphocyte activation (Rodríguez-Galán et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication supporting this claim.

claim: The putative mRNA targets of NK-EV-enriched miRNAs are involved in cellular development and movement, cell growth and proliferation, cell death, survival, and cell cycle.
source: Unbiased analysis of the pathways potentially affected by miRNAs shuttled into NK-EVs using the ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) revealed that the putative mRNA targets of NK-EV-enriched miRNAs were involved in cellular development and movement, cell growth and proliferation, cell death, survival, and cell cycle (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents results from IPA bioinformatics analysis of NK-EV miRNA targets.

claim: In silico mRNA target analyses for NK-EV-miRNAs identified putative target molecules related to immune signalling and Th1 responses, targeting CD4+ T lymphocytes and DCs among other immune effectors.
source: In silico mRNA target analyses for NK-EV-miRNAs identified putative target molecules related to immune signalling and Th1 responses, targeting CD4+ T lymphocytes and DCs among other immune effectors (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes in silico target prediction analysis with results provided in supplementary files.

claim: Most PtMs appeared at the edges of the canonical miRNA sequence, particularly at the terminal nucleotide (position 0) and the two flanking nucleotide positions (–1 and +1).
source: Most PtMs appeared at the edges of the canonical sequence, particularly at the terminal nucleotide (position 0) and the two flanking nucleotide positions (–1 and +1).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of post-transcriptional modifications from small RNA sequencing data.

claim: The 3p-end of miRNAs was significantly more prone to PtMs than the 5p-end in every sample.
source: The 3p-end of miRNAs was significantly more prone to PtMs (Figure 2A) than the 5p-end in every sample (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: The manuscript presents data comparing PtMs at 3p and 5p ends of miRNAs.

claim: Non-templated mono-additions of nucleotides were much more abundant than poly-additions.
source: Also, non-templated mono-additions of nucleotides were much more abundant than poly-additions (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents data comparing mono-additions and poly-additions of nucleotides to miRNAs.

claim: Cytosine addition was the most common modification, followed by adenine terminal insertions.
source: Cytosine addition was the most common modification, followed by adenine terminal insertions.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of nucleotide additions from small RNA sequencing data.

claim: Upon NK cell activation, miRNAs displayed reduced adenylation (positions −1, +1) and cytosylation (positions −1, +1).
source: Upon NK cell activation, miRNAs displayed reduced adenylation (positions −1, +1) and cytosylation (positions −1, +1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data comparing PtMs between resting and activated NK cells.

claim: Comparing activated NK cells with the NK-EVs they release, increased levels of cytosylated miRNA reads (positions 0, +1) and a decrease in guanosine additions (positions –1, 0) were detected.
source: Comparing activated NK cells with the NK-EVs they release, we detected increased levels of cytosylated miRNA reads (positions 0, +1), and a decrease in guanosine additions (positions –1, 0).
evidence: The manuscript presents data comparing PtMs between activated NK cells and their released EVs.

claim: MiRNAs specifically enriched in NK-EVs show a significantly higher proportion of isomiRs in NK-EVs than in their secreting-activated NK cells.
source: Remarkably, by analysing the percentage of reads with PtMs for the miRNAs specifically enriched in NK-EVs (Figure 2D, right panel), we found a significantly higher proportion of isomiRs in NK-EVs than in their secreting-activated NK cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of the fraction of miRNA reads with PtMs for NK-EV-enriched miRNAs.

claim: MiRNA molecules with PtMs are more likely to be included into EVs.
source: This suggests that miRNA molecules with PtMs are more likely to be included into EVs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observation that NK-EV-enriched miRNAs have higher proportions of PtMs.

claim: Five out of six of the most enriched NK-EV miRNAs show a higher number of reads with PtMs in NK-EVs compared to activated NK cells.
source: In fact, five out of six of the most enriched NK-EV miRNAs show a higher number of reads with PtMs in NK-EVs compared to activated NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the proportion of modified and unmodified miRNA reads for the most enriched NK-EV miRNAs.

claim: Both adenylation and cytosylation of canonical miRNA sequences accounted for the observed accumulation of PtMs in the NK-EV fraction.
source: We found that both adenylation and cytosylation of canonical miRNA sequences accounted for the observed accumulation of PtMs in the NK-EV fraction.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of specific nucleotide additions in NK-EV-enriched miRNAs.

claim: The levels of guanosylated miRNAs were very low in all samples, although more represented in resting NK cells.
source: The levels of guanosylated miRNAs were very low in all samples, although more represented in resting NK cells, while no significant differences were observed in the levels of uridine additions, among the samples analysed.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on guanosine and uridine additions to miRNAs across different samples.

claim: Accumulation of PtMs in miRNAs enriched in NK-EVs suggests an active PtMs-dependent mechanism of specific miRNA sorting into EVs.
source: Altogether, accumulation of PtMs in miRNAs enriched in NK-EVs suggests an active PtMs-dependent mechanism of specific miRNA sorting into EVs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the observed enrichment of post-transcriptionally modified miRNAs in NK-EVs.

claim: The accumulation of modified miRNAs in NK-EVs was not observed in the case of the most expressed NK-EV miRNAs, indicating additional layers of complexity in NK-EV-miRNA-specific packaging.
source: However, the accumulation of modified miRNAs in NK-EVs was not observed in the case of the most expressed NK-EV miRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating additional layers of complexity in NK-EV-miRNA-specific packaging, for example passive sorting of the most abundant miRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that the most highly expressed miRNAs do not show enrichment of PtMs in NK-EVs.

claim: Specific short sequence miRNA motifs are over-represented in EVs.
source: Specific short sequence miRNA motifs are over-represented in EVs (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript presents bioinformatics analysis identifying over-represented motifs in NK-EV miRNAs.

claim: Binding of specific motifs to RNA binding proteins, for example heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2/B1 (hnRNPA2B1), promotes miRNA sorting into EVs.
source: Binding of these motifs to RNA binding proteins, for example heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2/B1 (hnRNPA2B1), promotes miRNA sorting into EVs (Villarroya-Beltri et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature describing this mechanism.

claim: The short EV-associated motif GGAG identified in T cell-derived small EVs was over-represented in NK-EV-miRNAs.
source: Interestingly, the short EV-associated motif identified in T cell-derived small EVs GGAG was over-represented in NK-EV-miRNAs, and the tetra-nucleotide motif UGCA was also identified as a 'cell retention motif' in T cells, pointing towards similar mechanisms of miRNA sorting in lymphocytes(Garcia-Martin et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript presents bioinformatics analysis and cites previous literature on miRNA sorting motifs.

claim: Active targeting of specific miRNAs for EV release implies a putative role for these NK-EV-miRNAs in intercellular communication and regulatory functions.
source: Active targeting of specific miRNAs for EV release implies a putative role for these NK-EV-miRNAs in intercellular communication and regulatory functions.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the evidence of selective miRNA sorting into NK-EVs.

claim: An initial profiling of the cytokines secreted by NK-EV-treated CD4+ T cells in non-cytokine polarizing conditions showed high levels of Th1 function-related cytokines, including IFN-γ and IL-2.
source: An initial profiling of the cytokines secreted by NK-EV-treated CD4+ T cells in non-cytokine polarizing conditions showed high levels of Th1 function-related cytokines, including IFN-γ and IL-2 (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents cytokine profiling data from NK-EV-treated CD4+ T cells.

claim: No significant differences in overall CD4+ T cell survival were found after NK-EV treatment.
source: We found no significant differences in overall CD4+ T cell survival after NK-EV treatment.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data analyzing cell viability after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of isolated CD4+ T lymphocytes showed increased IFN-γ expression in the presence of NK-EVs in non-polarizing conditions.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of cultured CD4+ T cells showed an increase in the percentage of IFN-γ-producing T cells in the presence of NK-EVs in non-polarizing conditions.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased IFN-γ+ CD4+ T cells after NK-EV treatment.

claim: The effects of NK-EVs on IFN-γ production were not evident in Th1-polarizing conditions.
source: However, the effects were not evident in Th1-polarizing conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data comparing NK-EV effects in polarizing and non-polarizing conditions.

claim: Sandwich-ELISA analysis of cultured cells' supernatants revealed an increase in the levels of soluble IFN-γ in NK-EV-treated T cells in a non-cytokine-polarizing milieu.
source: Sandwich-ELISA analysis of cultured cells' supernatants revealed an increase in the levels of soluble IFN-γ in NK-EV-treated T cells in a non-cytokine-polarizing milieu (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents ELISA data measuring soluble IFN-γ in supernatants.

claim: Incubation with NK-EVs induced T-BET expression in non-cytokine-polarized T cells.
source: In addition, incubation with NK-EVs also induced T-BET expression in non-cytokine-polarized T cells (Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry and qPCR data showing increased T-BET expression after NK-EV treatment.

claim: NK-EV treatment correlated with a downregulation of GATA3 mRNA levels at day 3, which acts as a TBX21 suppressor.
source: correlating with a downregulation of the NK-EV miRNA target GATA3 mRNA levels at day 3, which acts as a TBX21 suppressor (Figure 3D,E; Gagliani and Huber, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing GATA3 downregulation and cites literature on GATA3's role as a TBX21 suppressor.

claim: The increase of T-BET protein levels and downregulation of GATA3 were confirmed by flow cytometry analyses after incubation with NK-EVs.
source: The increase of T-BET protein levels and downregulation of GATA3 were confirmed by flow cytometry analyses after incubation with NK-EVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data confirming T-BET upregulation and GATA3 downregulation.

claim: The increase of the NK-EV identified miRNAs miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p was confirmed by RT-qPCR in non-polarized culture conditions but not in cytokine Th1-polarizing cultures, after 3 days of incubation with NK-EVs.
source: The increase of the NK-EV identified miRNAs miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p, which have crucial functions in T cell responses (Supplementary file 2), was confirmed by RT-qPCR in non-polarized culture conditions but not in cytokine Th1-polarizing cultures, after 3 days of incubation with NK-EVs (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased levels of these miRNAs in CD4+ T cells after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Gold nanoparticles bearing a combination of miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p partially recapitulated the effects of NK-EVs in T-BET and GATA3 expression.
source: Three days after incubation with miRNA-bearing nanoparticles, the effects of NK-EVs in T-BET and GATA3 expression were partially recapitulated, indicating the involvement of these miRNAs in the observed phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data showing that nanoparticles carrying these miRNAs affect T-BET and GATA3 expression.

claim: NK-EV T cell uptake blockade using Dynasore abolished NK-EV-driven increase of IFN-γ expression.
source: NK-EV T cell uptake blockade using Dynasore abolished NK-EV-driven increase of IFN-γ expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), indicating the involvement of EV-uptake in promoting Th1-like responses.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing that blocking EV uptake prevents NK-EV effects on IFN-γ expression.

claim: SEC-isolated NK-derived small EVs showed a similar impact on IFN-γ expression as ultracentrifugation-isolated NK-EVs.
source: Despite a significant loss of NK-EV material during the SEC purification steps (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F), confirmed by a reduction of the exosomal markers CD81 and Tsg101 to around 20% of the levels obtained by ultracentrifugation, a similar impact for SEC-isolated NK-derived small EVs in IFN-γ expression was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G,H).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data comparing the effects of SEC-isolated and ultracentrifugation-isolated NK-EVs.

claim: Small EVs isolated from HEK-293 and Raji B lymphoblast cell lines showed no impact on IFN-γ secretion.
source: Finally, to rule out the non-specific effects of isolated EVs on T cell function, small EVs were isolated from two distinct human cell lines (namely the HEK-293, human epithelial kidney cells, and the Raji B lymphoblast cell lines), using our standard ultracentrifugation procedure. These vesicles showed no impact on IFN-γ secretion, that even decreased 6 days after incubation with Raji B cell-derived EVs, indicating the specificity of NK-EVs in skewing Th1 responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing that EVs from other cell types do not reproduce NK-EV effects.

claim: NK-EVs promoted T cell activation, as revealed by increased CD25 expression in non-polarizing conditions.
source: NK-EVs promoted T cell activation, as revealed by increased CD25 expression in non-polarizing conditions; whereas these effects were not further increased in a Th1 cytokine-polarized milieu (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased CD25 expression on CD4+ T cells after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Increased IL-2 release upon incubation with NK-EVs was confirmed by ELISA, 3 days after culture.
source: Increased IL-2 release upon incubation with NK-EVs was confirmed by ELISA, 3 days after culture (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents ELISA data measuring IL-2 in supernatants from NK-EV-treated T cells.

claim: Increased FOXP3 levels (p-value < 0.1) in non-polarized NK-EV-treated cells were observed compared to non-EV-treated cells.
source: Although no significant differences were found, increased FOXP3 levels (p-value < 0.1) in non-polarized NK-EV-treated cells were observed compared to non-EV-treated cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing a trend toward increased FOXP3 expression.

claim: IL10 secretion was not affected by NK-EV treatment, and was even reduced 3 days after culture in polarizing conditions.
source: However, IL10 secretion was not affected by NK-EV treatment, and was even reduced 3 days after culture in polarizing conditions.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing IL10 mRNA levels after NK-EV treatment.

claim: NK-EVs may limit suppressive Treg functions in Th1-skewing conditions.
source: These data suggest that additional levels of regulation participate in T cell responses, and that NK-EVs may limit suppressive Treg functions in Th1-skewing conditions.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observation that IL10 is reduced in polarizing conditions after NK-EV treatment.

claim: PTEN was downregulated by NK-EVs.
source: Functional regulatory molecules were downregulated by NK-EVs, including PTEN (Figure 4D), which is involved in T cell homeostasis
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing PTEN mRNA downregulation after NK-EV treatment.

claim: IL6 was reduced after NK-EV incubation (p-value <0.1).
source: Functional regulatory molecules were downregulated by NK-EVs, including PTEN (Figure 4D), which is involved in T cell homeostasis; IL6, which was reduced after NK-EV incubation (p-value <0.1)
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing a trend toward IL6 downregulation.

claim: TGFB and INPP5D genes were downregulated by NK-EVs.
source: Functional regulatory molecules were downregulated by NK-EVs, including PTEN (Figure 4D), which is involved in T cell homeostasis; IL6, which was reduced after NK-EV incubation (p-value <0.1); TGFB and INPP5D gene that encodes the SHIP1 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, D, F).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing downregulation of these genes after NK-EV treatment.

claim: The pleiotropic TNFA cytokine was upregulated shortly after NK-EV incubation in non-polarizing conditions, but decreased in Th1 cytokine-polarizing conditions.
source: On the contrary, the pleiotropic TNFA cytokine was upregulated shortly after NK-EV incubation in non-polarizing conditions, but decreased in Th1 cytokine-polarizing conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing differential TNFA expression depending on culture conditions.

claim: Dynamin-dependent endocytosis blockade using Dynasore confirmed the specific involvement of NK-EVs in T cell activation.
source: The specific involvement of NK-EVs in T cell activation was further confirmed after dynamin-dependent endocytosis blockade using Dynasore (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing that blocking EV uptake prevents NK-EV effects on CD25 expression.

claim: SEC-purified NK-EVs reproduced the effects on T cell activation observed with ultracentrifugation-isolated NK-EVs.
source: The specific involvement of NK-EVs in T cell activation was further confirmed after dynamin-dependent endocytosis blockade using Dynasore (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B) and reproduced with SEC-purified NK-EVs, despite the loss of material with this procedure (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data comparing effects of SEC-isolated and ultracentrifugation-isolated NK-EVs on CD25 expression.

claim: Incubation of T cells with either HEK or Raji-derived small EVs failed to reproduce NK-EV effects on CD25 expression.
source: Also, incubation of T cells with either HEK or Raji-derived small EVs failed to reproduce NK-EV effects, confirming the specificity of the observed phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing that EVs from other cell types do not increase CD25 expression.

claim: Raji-derived small EVs promoted a reduction in CD25 expression.
source: Interestingly, Raji-derived small EVs promoted a reduction in CD25 expression, indicating that NK-EV effects on T cells are not driven by small EVs from any lymphocyte.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing decreased CD25 expression after Raji-EV treatment.

claim: Although no significant differences were observed in cell survival and apoptosis, the presentation and costimulatory capacities of DCs were enhanced by NK-EVs exposure.
source: Flow cytometry analyses revealed that, although no significant differences were observed in cell survival and apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), the presentation and costimulatory capacities of DCs were enhanced by NK-EVs exposure (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing no change in viability but increased MHC-II and CD86 expression.

claim: Both NK-EV-treated monocytes and moDCs showed increased levels of MHC-II.
source: Indeed, both NK-EV-treated monocytes and moDCs showed increased levels of MHC-II (Figure 5A)
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased MHC-II expression on monocytes and moDCs after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Both NK-EV-treated monocytes and moDCs showed increased levels of the costimulatory CD86 molecule.
source: Indeed, both NK-EV-treated monocytes and moDCs showed increased levels of MHC-II (Figure 5A) and the costimulatory CD86 molecule (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased CD86 expression on monocytes and moDCs after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Non-cytokine-polarized monocytes exhibited a higher DC polarization, marked by an increased percentage of CD11c+DC-SIGN+ cells after incubation with NK-EVs.
source: Additionally, non-cytokine-polarized monocytes exhibited a higher DC polarization, marked by an increased percentage of CD11c+DC-SIGN+ cells after incubation with NK-EVs (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased CD11c+DC-SIGN+ cells after NK-EV treatment.

claim: NK-EVs' addition correlated with increased levels of IFN-γ and IL-12 secretion in monocytes, but not in moDCs that exhibited very low levels of these cytokines.
source: Interestingly, NK-EVs' addition correlated with increased levels of IFN-γ and IL-12 secretion in monocytes, but not in moDCs that exhibited very low levels of these cytokines (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased IFNG and IL12 mRNA in monocytes but not moDCs after NK-EV treatment.

claim: No significant expression differences were found for KLF13, FOXO1, NOTCH1, and VEGFR2 after treatment with NK-EVs in monocytes and moDCs.
source: Several putative targets for NK-EV miRNAs with important functions in DCs (Supplementary file 2) were analysed after treatment with NK-EVs, including KLF13, FOXO1, NOTCH1, and VEGFR2, but no significant expression differences were found (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing no significant changes in these genes after NK-EV treatment.

claim: Splenocytes isolated from nanoparticle-treated mice activated in vitro with anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies showed increased T cell activation after miRNA-bearing treatment compared to control nanoparticles, assessed by increased CD25 expression in CD4+ lymphocytes.
source: Interestingly, splenocytes isolated from nanoparticle-treated mice activated in vitro with anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies showed increased T cell activation after miRNA-bearing treatment compared to control nanoparticles, assessed by increased CD25 expression in CD4+ lymphocytes (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data from mouse splenocytes showing increased CD25 expression after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: qPCR analysis of total splenocytes showed increased mRNA levels of the Th1 hallmark Ifng after footpad administration of NK-EV miRNAs, in particular with miR-155 and a mixture of all three NK-EV miRNAs.
source: qPCR analysis of total splenocytes (Figure 6C) and popliteal draining lymph nodes (Figure 6D) showed increased mRNA levels of the Th1 hallmark Ifng after footpad administration of NK-EV miRNAs, in particular with miR-155 and a mixture of all three NK-EV miRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased Ifng mRNA in splenocytes after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: qPCR analysis of popliteal draining lymph nodes showed increased mRNA levels of Ifng after footpad administration of NK-EV miRNAs, in particular with miR-155 and a mixture of all three NK-EV miRNAs.
source: qPCR analysis of total splenocytes (Figure 6C) and popliteal draining lymph nodes (Figure 6D) showed increased mRNA levels of the Th1 hallmark Ifng after footpad administration of NK-EV miRNAs, in particular with miR-155 and a mixture of all three NK-EV miRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased Ifng mRNA in lymph nodes after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: Increased secretion of IFN-γ was confirmed in supernatants from in vitro-activated splenocytes by sandwich-ELISA.
source: Increased secretion of IFN-γ was also confirmed in supernatants from in vitro-activated splenocytes by sandwich-ELISA (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript presents ELISA data measuring IFN-γ in supernatants from splenocytes after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: T cells from mice treated with miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p exhibited a significantly enhanced expression of IFN-γ upon TCR-stimulation, compared to non-miRNA-treated cells.
source: Although no significant differences were found in the percentage of IFN-γ expressing CD4+ T cells (Figure 6F, lower panel), we could observe a similar tendency in T cells from mice treated with miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p, which exhibited a significantly enhanced expression of this cytokine upon TCR-stimulation, compared to non-miRNA-treated cells (Figure 6F, upper panel).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased IFN-γ MFI in CD4+ T cells after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: The effects of miR-10b-5p, miR-92a-3p, and miR-155-5p delivery in CD8+ T cells IFN-γ secretion were more robust than in CD4+ T cells.
source: The effects of miR-10b-5p, miR-92a-3p, and miR-155-5p delivery in CD8+ T cells IFN-γ secretion of this cytokine were more robust (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased IFN-γ expression in CD8+ T cells after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: The levels of Tbx21 were slightly increased in miRNA-treated mice, although the differences were not significant.
source: The levels of Tbx21 were slightly increased in miRNA-treated mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), although the differences were not significant, likely due to the kinetics of T-bet upregulation after Th1 commitment (Szabo et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing a trend toward increased Tbx21 and cites literature on T-bet kinetics.

claim: No differences were observed in the Treg compartment upon nanoparticle-based miRNA delivery, as addressed by the percentage of CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ cells.
source: Importantly, as observed in the experiments after NK-EV treatment in vitro, no differences were observed in the Treg compartment upon nanoparticle-based miRNA delivery, as addressed by the percentage of CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing no change in Treg populations after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: No differences in Il10 levels were observed in the spleen or popliteal draining lymph nodes after nanoparticle-based miRNA delivery.
source: Importantly, as observed in the experiments after NK-EV treatment in vitro, no differences were observed in the Treg compartment upon nanoparticle-based miRNA delivery, as addressed by the percentage of CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and the levels of Il10, neither in the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), nor in the popliteal draining lymph nodes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing no change in Il10 mRNA after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: ELISA analysis of supernatants from splenocytes from treated mice showed no significant differences in the levels of IL-2 secretion.
source: ELISA analysis of supernatants splenocytes from treated mice showed no significant differences in the levels of IL-2 secretion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents ELISA data showing no significant change in IL-2 secretion after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: Low levels of both IFN-γ and IL-2 cytokines were detected in serum from treated mice, however miR-10b-5p and miR-155-5p bearing nanoparticles promoted a slight increase of these cytokines.
source: Low levels of both IFN-γ and IL-2 cytokines were detected in serum from treated mice, however miR-10b-5p and miR-155-5p bearing nanoparticles promoted a slight increase of these cytokines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The manuscript presents ELISA data measuring cytokines in serum after nanoparticle-delivered miRNA treatment.

claim: Nanoparticles bearing three miRNAs preferentially excluded from the NK-EV fraction (hsa-miR-124, hsa-miR-3667, and hsa-miR-4518) showed no effects on T cell activation or IFN-γ secretion.
source: To further confirm the specificity of NK-EV-enriched miRNAs in promoting Th1 polarization and activation, AuNPs bearing three miRNAs preferentially excluded from the NK-EV fraction, namely hsa-miR-124, hsa-miR-3667, and hsa-miR-4518 were generated (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and their effects after footpad administration in immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice were evaluated, as for NK-EV miRNAs. These experiments showed no effects of these nanoparticles, as observed for NK-EV-enriched miRNAs. Neither activation nor IFN-γ secretion (Figure 6H) were affected by non-NK-EV miRNAs, further confirming the specificity of NK-EV miRNAs in the observed phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing that nanoparticles with non-NK-EV miRNAs do not affect T cell activation or IFN-γ expression.

claim: NK cell-derived exosomes mediate cytolytic effects on melanoma and neuroblastoma cells.
source: NK cell-derived exosomes mediate cytolytic effects on melanoma (Zhu et al., 2017) and neuroblastoma cells (Shoae-Hassani et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous publications describing these effects.

claim: NK cell-derived exosomes contain cytotoxic molecules such as Fas-L and perforin, which induce tumour cell apoptosis.
source: In addition, NK cell-derived exosomes contain cytotoxic molecules (Wu et al., 2019), such as Fas-L and perforin, which induce tumour cell apoptosis (Lugini et al., 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous publications describing the cytotoxic cargo of NK-EVs.

claim: DNAM1 is involved in exosome-mediated antitumoural responses.
source: or DNAM1 (Di Pace et al., 2020), which is also involved in exosome-mediated antitumoural responses, as revealed by experiments using blocking antibodies.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing DNAM1's role in NK-EV antitumor effects.

claim: NK-EVs have a beneficial effect in lung injury recovery after Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.
source: In particular, NK-EVs have a beneficial effect in lung injury recovery after Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing this effect.

claim: NK-EVs curb CCL4-induced liver fibrosis in mice by inhibiting TGF-β1-induced hepatic stellate cells activation.
source: NK-EVs curb CCL4-induced liver fibrosis in mice by inhibiting TGF-β1-induced hepatic stellate cells activation (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing this effect.

claim: miR-207-containing NK-EVs alleviate depression-like symptoms in mice.
source: Also, miR-207-containing NK-EVs alleviate depression-like symptoms in mice (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing this effect.

claim: miR-186 impaired neuroblastoma tumour growth and inhibited immune escape mechanisms by targeting the TGF-β pathway.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have identified the role of biologically active NK-EV miRNAs, such as miR-186, which impaired neuroblastoma tumour growth and inhibited immune escape mechanisms by targeting the TGF-β pathway (Neviani et al., 2019)
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing this miRNA's effects.

claim: miR-3607-3p inhibited pancreatic cancer, presumably by targeting its putative target IL-26.
source: or miR-3607-3p, which inhibited pancreatic cancer, presumably by targeting its putative target IL-26 (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing this miRNA's effects.

claim: NK cells promote T cell differentiation, proliferation, and cytokine production.
source: NK cells promote T cell differentiation, proliferation, and cytokine production (Crouse et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing NK cell effects on T cells.

claim: NK cell effects on T cells are mediated by direct interactions between NK and T lymphocytes; but also indirectly through their effect on antigen-presenting cells and the secretion of soluble factors.
source: These effects are mediated by direct interactions between NK and T lymphocytes; but also indirectly through their effect on antigen-presenting cells and the secretion of soluble factors.
evidence: The manuscript describes established mechanisms of NK cell-mediated T cell regulation.

claim: EVs carry bioactive molecules such as proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and genetic information, including microRNAs.
source: EVs, for example exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies, carry not only bioactive molecules such as proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, but also genetic information, including microRNAs (miRNAs) (Colombo et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing EV cargo.

claim: MiRNAs can be transferred among cells and modulate gene expression in the recipient cell.
source: These miRNAs can be transferred among cells and modulate gene expression in the recipient cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA function in intercellular communication.

claim: Dendritic cells are critical for the establishment of effective T cell responses.
source: Dendritic cells are critical for the establishment of effective T cell responses (Sallusto and Lanzavecchia, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing the role of dendritic cells.

claim: 3′ adenylation has been found to be over-represented in cells, while uridylation in exosomes from B cells suggesting a PtM-dependent specific cargo of miRNAs into small EVs.
source: PtMs of miRNAs have been previously reported to determine RNA fate and 3′ adenylation has been found to be over-represented in cells, while uridylation in exosomes from B cells suggesting a PtM-dependent specific cargo of miRNAs into small EVs (Koppers-Lalic et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing PtM patterns in cells and EVs.

claim: 3′uridylation is related to miRNA turnover during T cell activation.
source: Furthermore, 3′uridylation is related to miRNA turnover during T cell activation (Gutiérrez-Vázquez et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing this relationship.

claim: The post-transcriptional addition of non-templated nucleotides, particularly to the 3′ends of RNA molecules, is the most frequent and conserved RNA PtM.
source: The post-transcriptional addition of non-templated nucleotides, particularly to the 3′ends of RNA molecules, is the most frequent and conserved RNA PtM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNA post-transcriptional modifications.

claim: Non-templated nucleotide additions have an impact on miRNA stability, and gene regulation.
source: Interestingly, these modifications have an impact on miRNA stability, and gene regulation, thus on its regulatory capacities (Yu and Kim, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing the functional impact of PtMs.

claim: Changes in the miRNA repertoire during lymphocyte activation have been linked to their PtMs.
source: Since changes in the miRNA repertoire during lymphocyte activation have been linked to their PtMs (Rodríguez-Galán et al., 2021; Gutiérrez-Vázquez et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous publications describing this relationship.

claim: Many tumours dampen Th effector cell-mediated immunosurveillance.
source: In this regard, many tumours dampen Th effector cell-mediated immunosurveillance, and many immunotherapeutic approaches have focused in restoring Th1 responses (Knutson and Disis, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing tumor immune evasion mechanisms.

claim: Long-lasting effects of immune therapy are only observed in about 15% of cancer patients.
source: Immune therapy has revolutionized the treatment of cancer, however, long-lasting effects are only observed in about 15% of the patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the efficacy of current immunotherapy.

claim: Cancer immune evasion mechanisms include immune-suppressive mediators in the tumour microenvironment, impairment of CTL responses, promotion of T cell tolerance, and/or exhaustion and polarization from Th1 to Th2.
source: This might be due to the variety of cancer immune evasion mechanisms, including immune-suppressive mediators in the tumour microenvironment, impairment of CTL responses, promotion of T cell tolerance, and/or exhaustion and polarization from Th1 to Th2, among others (Marron et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing cancer immune evasion mechanisms.

claim: A large-scale NK-EV isolation protocol has been set up and may help translate into clinical therapies.
source: Interestingly, although primary human NK-EVs isolation may be tedious and time-consuming, a large-scale NK-EV isolation protocol has been set up and may help translate into clinical therapies (Jong et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing a large-scale isolation protocol.

claim: NK-EV-mediated immune deviation towards Th1 may be exploited when designing EV-based therapies.
source: Thus, we propose that NK-EV-mediated immune deviation towards Th1 may be exploited and taken into account when designing EV-based therapies.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this application based on the experimental findings.

claim: NK-EVs promote both directly and indirectly (via APCs) Th1 responses.
source: In summary, here, we provide new insights on the miRNA composition and impact of NK-EVs on immune responses, promoting both directly and indirectly (via APCs) Th1 responses.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main findings showing direct and indirect effects of NK-EVs on T cells.

claim: Unravelling the effects and mechanisms underlying NK-EV-mediated immune targeting, in particular Th2 to Th1 immune deviation, may help to improve therapeutic strategies.
source: Unravelling the effects and mechanisms underlying NK-EV-mediated immune targeting, in particular Th2 to Th1 immune deviation, may help to improve therapeutic strategies.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this potential application based on the findings.

claim: Specific miRNAs packaging into NK-EVs may involve different mechanisms, including non-templated nucleotide additions to miRNA canonical sequences and short-motif miRNA recognition by RNA-binding proteins.
source: Our analyses of NK-EV-enriched specific miRNAs suggest that specific miRNAs packaging into NK-EVs may involve different mechanisms, including non-templated nucleotide additions to miRNA canonical sequences and short-motif miRNA recognition by RNA-binding proteins.
evidence: The manuscript infers these mechanisms from the observed PtM patterns and motif enrichment in NK-EV miRNAs.

claim: NK-EV-miRNAs miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p uptake may promote GATA3 downregulation and subsequent T-bet de-repression, reprogramming recipient T cells towards the Th1 phenotype.
source: Thus, NK-EV miRNAs miR-10b-5p and miR-92a-3p uptake may promote GATA3 downregulation and subsequent T-bet de-repression, reprogramming recipient T cells towards the Th1 phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the observed effects of NK-EVs and nanoparticle-delivered miRNAs on GATA3 and T-bet expression.

claim: NK-EVs drive CD4+ T cell activation but do not significantly affect the Treg compartment.
source: In addition, NK-EVs drive CD4+ T cell activation, marked by increased CD25 expression and IL-2 production, but do not significantly affect the Treg compartment.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased CD25 and IL-2 but no significant changes in Foxp3 or IL-10.

claim: EVs do not only contain miRNAs, but also lipids and proteins that may contribute to the immunomodulatory effects of the NK-EVs.
source: It is important to highlight that EVs do not only contain miRNAs, but also lipids and proteins that also may contribute to the immunomodulatory effects of the NK-EVs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EV composition and the manuscript acknowledges this complexity.

claim: The presence of non-miRNA bioactive molecules in NK-EVs may account for some of the differences observed between the effects of synthetic miRNAs and NK-EVs.
source: The presence of these non-miRNA bioactive molecules in NK-EVs may account for some of the differences observed between the effects of synthetic miRNAs and NK-EVs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this explanation for the partial recapitulation of NK-EV effects by synthetic miRNAs.

claim: NK-EVs promote Th1 responses, both by directly targeting CD4+ T cells and by increasing APCs stimulating functions, necessary for the establishment of effective T cells responses.
source: Hence, NK-EVs promote Th1 responses, both by directly targeting CD4+ T cells and by increasing APCs stimulating functions, necessary for the establishment of effective T cells responses.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the dual mechanism of NK-EV action based on the experimental findings.
